claims.text: The starting as-cast or as-deposited BCC high-entropy alloy has a relatively coarse microstructure and limited intrinsic phase heterogeneity.
Combining laser melting deposition with post-deposition deep cryogenic treatment induces phase transitions in BCC Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys.
The combined LMD-DCT process refines grains and produces nanoscale precipitates.
Rapid solidification during LMD and DCT-induced changes in stresses and defects jointly generate multiscale microstructural heterogeneity.
DCT after LMD can improve tensile strength and elongation simultaneously in a BCC Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy.
DCT produces at least a 25% tensile-strength increase relative to an as-cast alloy.
DCT produces at least a 48% elongation increase relative to an as-cast alloy.
The 25% tensile-strength and 48% elongation improvements also apply relative to as-deposited material.
The combined treatment increases Young's modulus relative to as-cast or as-deposited material.
The combined treatment increases fracture resistance relative to as-cast or as-deposited material.
DCT promotes defect rearrangement in addition to phase transformation.
A network of dislocations and finer precipitates increases yield strength.
The proposed dislocation and precipitate structure arrests crack propagation and thereby improves fracture resistance.
Phase-transformation-induced symmetry breaking supplies additional slip systems that enhance ductility.
The resulting symmetry breaking produces a more uniform and higher Young's modulus.
Multiscale structural and compositional heterogeneities can underpin stable elastic-modulus behavior and other multifunctional properties in a high-entropy alloy.
The method should work only for dominant-BCC compositions sufficiently susceptible to cryogenically induced phase transformation.
Excessive cryogenic exposure can embrittle the alloy.
Direct evidence for Young's-modulus and fracture-resistance improvements under the proposed processing conditions is not yet provided.
A controlled comparison of otherwise equivalent LMD samples with and without DCT can test the hypothesis using tensile, modulus, fracture-toughness, and microscopy measurements.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires at least 25% higher tensile strength and 48% higher elongation, but the falsification rule only requires statistically significant improvements of unspecified magnitude. Small significant gains could therefore fail the quantitative prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
The baseline includes both as-cast and as-deposited material, whereas the proposed experiment compares two LMD-fabricated sets and therefore directly tests only the as-deposited control.
